body_markdown:
If today’s headline sounds a bit familiar, we’re paraphrasing a scene from the 1990 Dudley Moore movie, *Crazy People* . In that scene the advertising executive proposes a Volvo ad with the tagline, “Buy Volvos. They’re boxy but they’re good.” It was played for laughs, but the man was basically right. I should know: I grew up in them. In fact, I came home from the hospital in one—my mother’s dark blue 1977 245 DL station wagon.


Volvo


That wagon had originally been my dad’s company car, but when he got a 1979 Pontiac Bonneville sedan, he bought the Volvo from his company for Mom. We had that car for most of my early childhood, until it was replaced—with another boxy-but-good Volvo, a brand-new, pastel yellow 240 DL wagon special-ordered from Lundahl Motors. Michael Lundahl and his dad ran the dealership back then, and Mike and his wife were longtime friends of my folks.


Volvo


Back in the ’70s, there was really only one Volvo, once the 1800ES sport wagon was put out to pasture after 1973: the 200 series. It was, in effect, a heavily facelifted 140, with a new nose and McPherson strut front suspension. And they came in two flavors, the four-cylinder 240s and six-cylinder 260s, which first appeared in 1976 as the 264 GL. There was also a 265 DL wagon that year.


John De Dominicis Jr.


In the ’70s, the easiest way to tell a 260 from a 240 was the nose. The 1975-77 240s had a black horizontal bar grille and twin headlamps, while the early 260s had a more squared chrome grille with quad headlamps. Starting in 1978, most 240 models got the 260s-style grille and hood, with quad round headlamps, but at the same time, the 260s got quad rectangular headlights. And the 260s always had a chrome grille.


John De Dominicis Jr.


For 1979, the 260 series, which consisted of the sedan, wagon, and 262C coupe by Bertone, had a B27F “PRV” V-6, so named because the engine was a joint development between Peugeot, Renault, and Volvo. The 163 cubic-inch unit produced 127 horsepower at 5500 rpm, and 146 lb-ft of torque at 2750 rpm.


John De Dominicis Jr.


At the time, all Volvos had a 12-month limited warranty with no mileage restriction. All models rolled on Michelin steel-belted radial tires. All 240/260 models had a 104-inch wheelbase and overall length of 192.5 inches. And the wagons, as expected, had ample cargo space, to the tune of 41.1 cubic feet—which increased to 76 cubic feet with the rear seat folded down.


John De Dominicis Jr.


Today’s car was seen at the Das Awkscht Fescht (that translates to The August Festival) in Macungie, Pennsylvania this summer by my friend and fellow car nut, John De Dominicis, Jr. He posted some pics of it on his social media, and I must have left an enthusiastic reply, because he sent me several more pics! After that, it was just a matter of finding my 1979 Volvo brochures, and voila!


John De Dominicis Jr.


Thanks, John. You made me flash back to playing in the front seat of Mom’s ’77 wagon back when I was maybe five, and dropping coins down the air conditioning vents. I do believe I got in trouble for that, but it certainly cured me from ever doing that again!


John De Dominicis Jr.


As for Mom’s blue wagon, it was, after the delivery of the new yellow 1986 wagon, sold to a friend of my father’s. He was notoriously rough on his cars, but as I recall he drove it at least another four or five years before he finally replaced it. It’s like the old ads used to say: Drive it like you hate it, it’s OK, because the Volvo can take whatever you dish out!


John De Dominicis Jr.
